thread.title: Shareholder Pressure Might Be Driving Qualcomm to Talk With Broadcom - TheStreet

author: Eric Jhonsa
title: Shareholder Pressure Might Be Driving Qualcomm to Talk With Broadcom - TheStreet
text:
After sliding last week as Broadcom ( AVGO ) lowered its offer price for the company following a revised deal to buy NXP ( NXPI ) , Qualcomm's ( QCOM ) shares are up about 6% this week and within $3 of a 52-week high (set in November) of $69.28.
Though a slew of product and design-win announcements made at the Mobile World Congress (MWC) haven't hurt, it's safe to assume that the latest press releases and media reports related to Broadcom's bid are the main factors behind Qualcomm's gains. In particular, two pieces of news appear to have given Qualcomm's shares a lift:
On Monday morning, Qualcomm published an open letter from chairman Paul Jacobs stating that Qualcomm and Broadcom have "made progress on regulatory and other deal certainty issues." But he added that the companies remain at odds over price and Broadcom's refusal to disclose its post-acquisition plans for Qualcomm's licensing business, which remains in disputes with multiple regulators, Apple ( AAPL ) and a major Android licensee. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan has said he sees opportunities to "rationalize and restructure" Qualcomm's licensing business. Jacobs also said Qualcomm is interested in further talks, and -- as part of a 4-part negotiation process it wants to pursue -- is delivering a proposed non-disclosure agreement (NDA) to Broadcom's lawyers that would let each company see the other's books. The Financial Times reported that Qualcomm has "dropped its objections" to being acquired by Broadcom and is open to a deal featuring a price above $90 per share (over $160 billion after accounting for debt). That spells a premium of at least 14% relative to Broadcom's $79 per share offer price , and a 65%-plus premium to where Qualcomm traded last October before the first reports of a Broadcom bid emerged. None of this necessarily means a deal will shortly be inked. Broadcom declared Jacobs' letter to be " engagement theater ," and said it doesn't believe the process outlined by Qualcomm "is designed to lead to a prompt agreement." It once more called on Qualcomm shareholders to back Broadcom's efforts to take control of Qualcomm's board through a six-director slate at the company's March 6 annual meeting.

Qualcomm responded by calling Broadcom's PR "disingenuous," and insisted it "has repeatedly attempted to engage with Broadcom on issues including price, including at meetings on February 14 and February 23." The company also declared it has no plans to postpone its annual meeting, and claimed Broadcom is the party that has "refused to engage on price."
But for all the mudslinging between the companies, Qualcomm's stance does appear to have changed some since last November, when it unequivocally rejected Broadcom's original $70 per share offer on account of both its price and antitrust risks. Qualcomm's attitude does appear to have shifted, both in terms of suggesting that regulatory risks can be addressed, and voicing a willingness to engage in advanced deal talks centered around price.
Shareholder pressure might be forcing the hand of a Qualcomm management team that's reluctant to sell to a company that has earned a reputation for aggressively cutting spending at firms it acquires. Broadcom's $79 per share offer -- $57 per share in cash and $22 per share in stock -- represents a 45% premium to Qualcomm's $54.38 closing price on the day before the first reports of Broadcom's bid emerged, something that can't be lost on major Qualcomm investors ahead of the annual meeting.
To be fair, if Qualcomm was to agree to Broadcom's offer, its share might only rise to the mid-70s, given the antitrust risk surrounding the deal and the fact that full regulatory clearance --assuming it was to happen -- probably wouldn't occur before mid-2019. And if Broadcom was to walk away, Qualcomm shares might only drop to the high 50s, given greater certainty about the closing of the deal for NXP, and the company's presentation of a roadmap for achieving strong near-term EPS growth with NXP's help.
But that still spells a price delta of 25% or more between the two outcomes. Even for shareholders who are quite bullish on Qualcomm's prospects as a standalone company, that's not easy to walk away from. That's particularly so given Broadcom's stellar M&A execution history and the many cost and product synergies a deal could deliver. It's worth noting here that one major shareholder advisory firm (Glass Lewis) is backing Broadcom's director slate, while another (ISS) recommends 4 out of 6 directors.
Moreover, Broadcom could conceivably up its offer for Qualcomm a bit prior to the annual meeting to win over shareholders who are on the fence. Whereas the company once called its $82 per share bid ($60 per share in cash) for Qualcomm its "best and final offer" for the company, it hasn't used similar language to describe the $79 per share offer made following the revised NXP deal. In his letter to Broadcom, Jacobs noted that Broadcom has insisted its latest offer its "best and final proposal," but Broadcom hasn't made such comments in its public remarks.
One possibility here is that Broadcom, which is already committing to raising a massive amount of debt to absorb Qualcomm and NXP, ups the stock portion of its offer by a few dollars. That would result in Broadcom shares, which have more than doubled since early 2016, accounting for close to a third of the deal's payout.
If that happens, the pressure to make a deal rises further still -- regardless of any reservations that Qualcomm's management has about handing a company with a long history of mobile radio and chip innovation over to Hock Tan and his team of cost-cutters.
